title: Bridging ELIXIR nodes for collaborative and scalable BYOC in Galaxy and TREs
abstract: This project builds on the capabilities of the de.NBI Cloud, extending its SimpleVM infrastructure to support advanced Bring Your Own Compute (BYOC) for Galaxy. By integrating automated infrastructure provisioning with scalable Pulsar execution backends, we aim to enable seamless integration of dedicated compute resources to Galaxy. Building on prior work from EOSC EuroScienceGateway, the project introduces a unified approach that supports both fully managed and user-managed scenarios. In the fully managed model, infrastructure components such as Pulsar, SLURM, and storage are automatically provisioned and integrated. In parallel, user-managed setups are facilitated through automation via Galaxy APIs and CI pipelines, providing flexibility while maintaining reproducibility and ease of use. Beyond its implementation within de.NBI Cloud, this framework is designed to be utilized by Galaxy providers across ELIXIR Nodes and cloud providers. By standardizing the integration of external compute resources, it bridges distributed infrastructures and connects ELIXIR Nodes, enabling them to collaboratively offer scalable BYOC capabilities and shared access to heterogeneous compute environments. In parallel, the project will investigate how such infrastructures can support secure processing environments (TRE/SPE) and interoperate with existing solutions such as SURF's Tinker SANE. By leveraging shared technologies (e.g., web-based remote access, reproducible VM images), we aim to enable portable, secure, and user-specific virtual research environments. The outcome will be a framework that simplifies the onboarding of external compute resources into Galaxy, improves scalability, supports sensitive data use cases, and fosters collaboration across ELIXIR Nodes and cloud providers.
leads: Sanjay Kumar Srikakulam, Mirela Minkova, Vipin Thankam Sreedharan

title: Enhancing AI-readiness of multi-modal data submission: a reference workflow
abstract: This project will produce a fully documented, end-to-end reference workflow for multi-modal data submission using the MARS approach, to be published as an article and FAIR outputs. It builds on an existing operational prototype pipeline that integrates ISA-JSON for structured metadata exchange with data transfer and orchestration mechanisms, including dedicated test/beta programmatic submission endpoints provided by ELIXIR Deposition Database (EDD). The workflow demonstrates how heterogeneous life science datasets can be submitted in a reproducible and programmatic manner, combining metadata handling, data dispatch, and large-scale transfer within a single coherent process. The main goal is not to generate new datasets, but to systematically execute and document this workflow to enable reuse and adoption across ELIXIR Nodes. A key outcome is a clear, step-by-step reference implementation that improves dataset interlinking and supports more consistent metadata structures, thereby increasing the AI-readiness of deposited datasets compared to current heterogeneous submission practices. The project will also identify current gaps in automation, interoperability, and metadata harmonisation, providing concrete recommendations for future improvements. All materials, including code, documentation, and structured metadata examples, will be released in a reusable and FAIR-compliant manner. The resulting publication will serve as a practical blueprint for Node-based implementations and contribute to the development of a Multi-Node Toolbox for interoperable multi-omics data submission workflows.
leads: Flora D'Anna, April Shen, Dipayan Gupta

title: Developing Open Standards for a Semantic Framework in Plant Specialized Metabolism
abstract: Plant specialized metabolites are a major source of innovative pharmaceuticals, novel foods, and biobased natural products. However, resolving the metabolic pathways that biosynthesize these compounds remains a key scientific challenge, as plant biosynthetic genes are often genomically dispersed and duplicated, resulting in highly branched, diversified, and promiscuous underlying metabolic networks. Additionally, knowledge of plant metabolic pathway knowledge remains scattered across disconnected resources, with limited interoperable annotations, and valuable experimental multi-omics datasets remain siloed and underused. To address these gaps, we developed the Linked Open Data knowledge graph PlantMetWiki (https://plantmetwiki.bioinformatics.nl/), the first semantically enriched knowledge base for querying experimentally validated pathway information for plant biosynthetic reactions, including predictions of biosynthetic gene clusters. Still, researchers lack an open, standardized, and reusable AI-ready format for integrating new datasets with community knowledge. Additionally, there is no framework to systematically link computational evidence from bioinformatics tools and paired plant transcriptomics-metabolomics datasets to predict or validate pathway-level knowledge. Therefore, in this BioHackathon project, we aim to: 1) Co-develop a community-supported Minimum Information Standard (MIS) for predicted plant pathway knowledge representation; 2) Design validation schemas to integrate experimental multi-omics datasets and predictions in alignment with the MIS; 3) Establish methods to align pathway-related predictions across bioinformatics pipelines and approaches for scoring and prioritization of these predictions based on evidence strength, provenance, and community-defined criteria. These outcomes will enable scalable community annotation of pathway information, improved integration of multi-omics data, prioritization of candidate pathway components, and more reproducible and transparent bioinformatics analyses.
leads: Elena Del Pup, Denise Slenter, Kumar Saurabh Singh

title: Establishing a Flexible Open-Source Modeling System for Population-Scale Biology
abstract: Large biobanks contain vast amounts of genomic and phenotypic data that could help reveal the etiologies of prevalent clinical phenotypes such as Alzheimer’s disease or cancer. Despite the availability of these resources, they cannot be easily shared and combined across institutions due to privacy restrictions. We propose to establish a flexible open-source modeling framework that enables the community to combine publicly available biobank data and other datasets while preserving individuals’ privacy. In this project, we will build a network-based pipeline for integrating biobank data within knowledge graphs and further subtyping of individuals to identify etiological factors of complex diseases. We will extend our project from the ELIXIR BioHackathon 2025, in which we introduced a methodology for the modeling of genotype-phenotype interactions based on genomic hashes. We implemented it as a ready-to-use bioinformatics pipeline and showed that it is capable of fast and scalable genome comparisons using public data. Extending this work at the ELIXIR BioHackathon 2026, in collaboration with several European and international biobanks, will pave the way for responsible data federation across biobanks and support the development and administration of maximally effective targeted therapeutic strategies. In addition, it will allow us to implement our approach within a standardized infrastructure, ensuring accessibility and visibility for a number of important stakeholders.
leads: Ben Busby, Jedrzej Kubica, Mauricio Moldes

title: A submission and visualisation interface for sharing community interoperability practices
abstract: Interoperability practices across stakeholder groups, whether through projects, institutes, platforms or communities, are often shared as informal know-how in slides, wikis, or email threads, making them hard to find, compare, improve and reuse. Building on an ongoing ELIXIR Interoperability Platform (EIP) effort to collect practices using the RDMkit Data Life Cycle framing, this project will develop a lightweight submission and visualisation interface to share reference community practices across the research data management ecosystem. The project builds on an existing questionnaire, currently undertaken as a “guided” interview, that already captures the key elements to enable the “FAIR” re-execution of a “task”, including domain or context, lifecycle stage, tools and resources used, and key constraints. We will turn this into a guided workflow that allows stakeholders (ELIXIR members, community champions, data stewards, etc) to submit practices directly, without needing an interview. Submitted practices will be exportable in machine-readable formats such as JSON and YAML, and displayed in human-friendly views such as data lifecycle maps, comparison tables, and tool-assembly-style diagrams. The prototype will include examples from several ELIXIR communities and link to relevant resources such as RDMkit, the FAIR Cookbook, FAIRsharing, bio.tools, github, etc. By making it easier for communities to contribute, find and reuse interoperability-enhanced practices, the interface will help them identify shared solutions, spot gaps, and move more quickly toward interoperable workflows, tools, and metadata approaches.
leads: Tooba Abbassi-Daloii, Nick Juty, Bilgehan Nevruz

title: Implementing Credit and Recognition for Research Outputs Beyond Publications in ELIXIR
abstract: Research in the life sciences depends on many outputs beyond traditional publications, including datasets, databases, software, and workflows. These outputs result from a diverse range of specialized activities - such as data curation, software engineering, training - that currently lack structured technical pathways for formal recognition. However, the technical infrastructure for representing and recognising contributions to these outputs remains fragmented, limiting visibility for contributors and reducing incentives for sustainable resource maintenance. This project will develop practical technical building blocks for a credit and recognition framework for ELIXIR resources. The project has three linked activities: 1. We will identify, reuse, and enhance existing standards to define an extended vocabulary of contributor roles. This effort focuses on capturing the nuanced activities and expertise required to produce non-traditional research outputs, ensuring that these contributions are accurately represented and interoperable across ELIXIR services. 2. We will develop a technical recognition model useful to the ELIXIR Platforms and implementation guidelines for resource managers, covering contribution events, provenance, attribution, aggregation, and reuse. 3. We will expand the integration of APICURON and BIP! Scholar with GitHub to transform raw signals (pull requests, issues, releases) into structured recognition events. This provides a direct credit pathway for any ELIXIR resource reliant on git-based contributions, e.g. software tools and training materials. Where feasible, we will also identify candidate KPIs to assess coverage, uptake, interoperability, and usefulness of the framework. Expected outputs: * Include a draft controlled vocabulary * Implementation recommendations * A prototype APICURON-GitHub workflow for the discussed activities * Initial KPIs to assess framework uptake
leads: Federica Quaglia, Hervé Ménager, Maria Makaronidou

title: PhyloAI: Extending a Machine Learning-Based Quartet Topology Classifier for Phylogenomic-Scale Tree Reconstruction
abstract: Phylogenetic inference is a central tool in biology and bioinformatics. Current methods (most commonly used are maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference) face computational challenges due to the ever-growing size of genomic datasets. To address these limitations, we developed PhyloAI, a machine learning method trained on alignment site pattern frequency distributions that reconstructs phylogenetic trees with high accuracy while being up to five orders of magnitude faster than maximum likelihood methods. PhyloAI takes a multiple sequence alignment as an input, predicts the tree topology for every quartet in the alignment using the existing pre-trained neural networks and amalgamates quartet trees with ASTRAL/wQFM to reconstruct a larger a N-taxon phylogenetic tree. In this BioHackathon project, we will extend our working version of PhyloAI by introducing explicit filtering of unreliable quartets, using either reconstructibility predictor networks or softmax-based confidence estimates. By reducing the impact of incorrectly inferred quartets, this step is expected to substantially improve overall tree accuracy. Finally, we aim to make PhyloAI broadly accessible by developing a fully packaged and user-friendly software distribution available via pip and conda.
leads: Nikita Kulikov, Christoph Mayer, Iker Irisarri

title: Advancing Research Software Quality across ELIXIR: Sustainable, Reproducible, and Interoperable Life-Science Software
abstract: This project aims to evaluate and enhance research software (RS) quality dimensions, indicators, and best practices to support sustainable, reliable, and reproducible research across ELIXIR Nodes. Assessing RS quality remains a major challenge in the Life Sciences, where software plays a central role in data analysis, integration, and interpretation. At the same time, the principles underpinning RS quality are broadly applicable across the wider research ecosystem, including the European Health Data Space (EHDS) and other EOSC science domains. European initiatives such as B1MGplus, EVERSE, and ELIXIR-STEERS highlight the growing consensus on the need for coordinated approaches and provide a strong foundation for this work. The project will review, map, and prioritise research software quality indicators most relevant to the ELIXIR infrastructure and related initiatives, including the One Million Genomes (1+MG). It will build on existing community-driven efforts, including the quality dimensions and indicators developed during BioHackathon 2024, their further development in EVERSE, and the good practices promoted by ELIXIR-STEERS. Particular attention will be given to well-described metadata, compliance, risk assessment, and alignment across different software tiers to reflect varying levels of maturity. The project will also consider the broader operational context, including infrastructures such as secure processing environments, especially relevant to 1+MG and EHDS. This work is directly relevant to the ELIXIR Tools Platform, where efforts are ongoing to define and implement approaches for assessing software quality. The workshop will contribute to these activities by aligning proposed indicators with Tools Platform needs and strengthening connections with EVERSE.
leads: Laura Portell-Silva, Shoaib Sufi, Styliani-Christina Fragkouli

title: From alignment to insight: synchronized MSA and 3D structure visualization
abstract: Every biologist has stared at a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and wondered: what do these conserved columns actually mean in 3D? For decades the answer required structural expertise or a painful context-switch into specialist tools. AlphaFold, ESMFold, and Foldseek have made high-quality structure ensembles available for virtually any protein family — yet the visualization paradigm hasn't kept up. We still compare structures the way we did 40 years ago: backbone superpositions, ribbon diagrams, cluttered ensemble views that experts navigate by instinct and non-experts simply cannot use. This project closes that gap. In five days we will build an open-source, browser-based tool that takes a standard MSA (FASTA or CLUSTALW) alongside protein structures and produces a synchronized, clutter-free view: conservation and divergence mapped directly onto molecular surfaces, with the 1D alignment and 3D view locked in sync. Conserved drug-binding pockets light up. Divergent interaction surfaces stand out. No structural expertise required. Building on the Mol*/iCn3D MolViewSpec bridge from BioHackathon Europe 2025, we deliver: (1) a one-click ensemble comparison demo across GPCRs, Tyrosine Kinases, and Immunoglobulins, (2) a reusable surface-mapping API, (3) a web UI where you load your own MSA and structures and get a publication-ready visualization in seconds, and (4) LLM-assisted alignment, analysis, and reporting — turning static comparisons into living narratives. If you work with protein families, drug targets, or AlphaFold clusters and have ever wished your alignment could show you the biology — this project is for you. Sequence biologists, structural bioinformaticians, tool developers, and students all welcome.
leads: Adam Midlik, Philippe Youkharibache, David Sehnal

title: Enabling workflows and EDAM annotations to display in community website deployments
abstract: The ELIXIR Toolkit Theme (ETT) enables communities to deploy websites via GitHub, facilitating broad contributions and collaborations, and streamlining the process of building and populating the site. The popularity of the ETT is demonstrated by numerous deployments, including RDMkit, RSQkit, and WorkflowHub documentation. These deployments can also centralise sharing of digital resources such as workflows intended for reuse by communities. This use case requires a streamlined way to find, view, and understand workflows, in the context of an ETT deployed website. Whilst ETT already offers the possibility of annotating pages with identifiers from FAIRsharing and bio.tools, support for workflows and ontologies is not implemented. This project will extend the ETT to enable 1) automation of workflow imports from WorkflowHub, 2) creation of interactive tables to present the communities workflows, and 3) automated addition of EDAM ontology annotations at both the workflow table and webpage (i.e. schema.org) level. The latter will build on the existing integration with bio.tools, offer the possibility of manual curation, and increase the findability of these webpages. Moreover, ontology terms (e.g. EDAM) are already used to annotate the bio.tools elements already included on many ETT instances, including RDMkit. Workflow developers from any community can thus continue using WorkflowHub to make their workflows FAIR, and community coordinators can independently and automatically import these to an ETT deployment along with EDAM annotations. This support would be beneficial for increasing the findability of the pages and enabling better integration across multiple instances of ETT.
leads: Federico Bianchini, Joshua Baskaran, Johan Gustafsson

title: VERDANT: Vocabulary Enrichment & Resolution of Diversity Annotations via Neural Technology
abstract: Biodiversity and microbiome research increasingly depends on knowledge graphs (KGs) to integrate heterogeneous data across genomic, environmental, and ecological domains. Yet populating these KGs with high-quality semantic links to external ontologies remains a manual, error-prone bottleneck. Existing tools handle ontology construction or querying, but none provide an end-to-end, AI-driven pipeline that automatically scrapes authoritative term sets, builds formal OWL 2 ontologies, and generates confidence-scored SKOS mappings to multiple knowledge bases simultaneously. VERDANT addresses this gap with a production-ready, reusable tool that transforms any structured vocabulary into a FAIR, interlinked ontology layer. The pipeline uses SentenceTransformer embeddings with FAISS vector indexing to produce semantic mappings (exactMatch, closeMatch, relatedMatch) to Wikidata, DBpedia, ENVO, NCBITaxon, and other targets. An expert pre-check interface enables domain specialists to validate AI suggestions, with their decisions feeding back as training data to iteratively improve the classifier. At BioHackathon 2026, we will demonstrate VERDANT on the Natura 2000 protected-area vocabulary (1,955 EU-mandated biodiversity terms, 14,500+ mappings already generated) while generalising the tool for reuse by other communities. Concretely, we will deploy a federated SPARQL endpoint, build API connectors to BioPortal, TeSS, and GBIF, prototype the expert validation and AI fine-tuning infrastructure, and validate cross-domain applicability by enriching a subset of the ELIXIR Microbiome Community's Knowledge Graph. All outputs are MIT-licensed and containerised with Docker Compose.
leads: Jovana Dobreva, Miguel Rodriguez Rojas, James McLaughlin

title: SampleSift: spatial querying and selection of geolocation-tagged biological samples
abstract: Multiple ELIXIR Core Data Resources (CDRs), including ENA and MGnify, hold vast collections of biological samples with geographic coordinates, driven by exponential data growth and enforced metadata requirements. Yet spatial exploration remains limited: existing tools offer only basic geographic query builders, requiring further code to combine them with advanced metadata filtering or prepare intuitive data visualisations. These limitations extend to myriad resources both within and outside ELIXIR communities, for example where relevant data are deposited to generic data repositories like Zenodo, or in bespoke data portals. Emerging data resources built on-top of existing reusable codebases and infrastructures are destined to inherit these limitations. SampleSift will address this gap with a modular, open-source stack of technologies for spatially querying and filtering large biological sample collections. A database layer of spatial-specific tooling (e.g. PostGIS for Postgres, SpatiaLite for SQLite) is paired with an interactive Leaflet.js map interface, allowing users to draw geographic regions of interest and retrieve matching samples in real time, filtered simultaneously by taxonomy, collection date, environment biome, and other metadata dimensions. The architecture is explicitly designed for scale (e.g. 100,000+ records) and for reuse: the embeddable map widget, RESTful faceted search API, and spatial query layer can each be adopted independently by any web data portal. We intend for MGnify, ELIXIR’s CDR for microbiome-derived data, to be an exemplar use case. This hackathon will deliver a live prototype on real CDR data, a reusable map widget, an OpenAPI-documented faceted search API, and containerised deployment documentation.
leads: Aleksandar Rajković, Angel Phanthanourak, Alexander Rogers

title: ELIXIR AI Ecosystem Integration: Bridging DOME, BioAIrepo and Galaxy
abstract: The adoption of machine learning in the life sciences has been transformative, solving landmark challenges and accelerating research. However, researchers face an ongoing reproducibility and reusability crisis. While foundational resources like the DOME Registry for method disclosure and the BioAIrepo for dataset and model deposition exist, a critical functional gap remains between identifying an AI asset and successfully executing it. This project aims to bridge that gap by functionally integrating the ELIXIR AI ecosystem. Firstly, we will establish a scalable proof-of-concept mechanism to run models directly from the DOME Registry and BioAIrepo via Galaxy. By landscaping existing BioModels ML mechanisms, we will implement front-end features enabling seamless model execution. Secondly, we will jointly enhance interoperability between these resources. Leveraging indexed assets from EBI Search federation, we will successfully pull in and cross-link related software assets from Europe PMC and bio.tools to their corresponding method and data entries in the DOME Registry and BioAIrepo. Finally, to support researchers in navigating this unified landscape, we will develop improved unified submission documentation and user guidance. This content will explicitly bridge the transition from asset identification to execution. It will be published as a dedicated RDMkit page to ensure optimal viewership and will align with established DOME and OSAI guidelines. Ultimately, this project will streamline AI model discovery and execution, ensuring ELIXIR infrastructures provide highly actionable, cross-linked resources for the scientific community.
leads: Gavin Farrell, Eliot Ragueneau, Anup Kumar

title: Unlocking Animal Data for Reproducible Research with ARC RO–Crate
abstract: This project aims to bridge critical gaps in the implementation of the ISA (Investigation, Study, Assay) model for animal phenotyping by advancing its practical usability. Although last year’s hackathon project confirmed the ISA model’s suitability for animal phenotyping, its adoption remains hindered by the lack of user-friendly tools and incomplete implementation. The Plant Science Community has already developed, within the NFDI consortium DataPLANT, a RO-Crate-based Annotated Research Context (ARC) ecosystem that fosters phenotypic ISA models for plants. The re-use of these structures not only enables the efficient implementation of a usable standard for the animal data community but also represents a first step towards an extended data format in the agricultural sector. The core objective of the project is to set up an ARC for animals with its associated software, like the ARCitect or ISA Wizard, to support intuitive, standardized annotation of ISA-aligned animal phenotypic data. In this process, the new animal-related terms from the ISA checklist need to be integrated or adapted into the software. Therefore, a pilot dataset of animal phenotypic data will be generated and packaged as an ARC, demonstrating the end-to-end workflow from data collection to FAIR-compliant curation. The outcome will be a validated, accessible software tool suite that enables researchers to easily annotate, manage, and share animal phenotyping data in alignment with FAIR principles. This work will significantly enhance reproducibility, data integration, and cross-study comparisons in animal research, laying the groundwork for broader adoption of the ISA model in the life sciences.
leads: Rica Rehfeld, Manuel Feser, Emily Clark

title: From dream to reality: a knowledge graph of learning resources in practice
abstract: Training registries such as TeSS and Glittr.org contain a rich body of metadata describing training materials, events, and contributors across the life‑science and biomedical domains. Although this information is represented in RDF, it remains insufficiently interconnected with other knowledge resources and is not easily discoverable or queryable by end users or automated systems. As a result, much of its potential value for learners, trainers, and research infrastructure professionals remains untapped. This project will deliver a publicly available, continuously updated knowledge graph (KG) for training resources. The training KG will be made available alongside major Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics (SIB) knowledge graphs within the Expasy ecosystem. This co‑location will allow users to query and explore training data using the same tools, interfaces, and usage patterns they already employ for other available resources. We will focus on improving data quality, interoperability, and reusability across existing training registries. Author identification and attribution will be strengthened by leveraging persistent identifiers such as ORCID, enabling rich, reusable contributor profiles, while shared schemas will be used to harmonize metadata. By following SIB best practices for exposing SPARQL endpoints, including example queries and clear schemas, the KG will be FAIR, self-describing, and easily reusable by downstream users and services. A key innovation is enabling direct interaction with the linked data through a conversational interface. The training KG will be federated within the Expasy portal alongside resources such as UniProt and Bgee, improving cross‑resource discovery, visibility, and sustainability, supporting reuse by humans and agents.
leads: Phil Reed, Panayiotis Smeros, Vincent Emonet

title: MiCoKnowGraph: Designing a Microbiome Collaborative Knowledge Graph linking complex, multi-domain data
abstract: Microbiome research generates complex, multi-domain data, spanning genomic, imaging, metabolic, clinical, and environmental contexts. While recent initiatives have demonstrated the potential of knowledge graphs (KGs) to map bacteria-host interactions and microbiome-disease associations, these efforts remain fragmented and non-interoperable across disparate resources. To address this bottleneck, we propose the conceptual and architectural design of a unified microbiome KG, led by the ELIXIR Microbiome Community. This BioHackathon project focuses on foundational data modelling to integrate heterogeneous ecosystems and foster connections with Biodiversity, Health, Food & Nutrition communities. Given the complexity of mapping multi-omic, imaging, and other data, our primary objective is to collaboratively design a scalable, interoperable KG schema. Participants will identify existing KGs and essential entities, such as taxonomic units, (functional) genes, metabolites, diseases, and habitats, and define their formal semantic relationships by evaluating and mapping established ontologies (e.g., Gene Ontology, ENVO, DO, SOSA, SIO, NCIT, UBERON, EFO, DCT). The designed KG will be partly implemented in collaboration with the VERDANT proposed project. The community will evaluate this consensus-driven architecture by designing query templates for four use cases: aeromicrobiome functional characterisation, antimicrobial resistance transmission, host-microbiome interactions in cancer, and the metabolic impact of nutrition. By delivering a formalised blueprint, this project will empower researchers to harmonise existing KGs and unlock actionable insights from complex ecosystems.
leads: Nikolaos Strepiis, Bérénice Batut, Brieuc Quemeneur

title: Bridging Literature and Practice: Tool Co-citation Networks from Publications and Registered Workflows
abstract: InSoLiTo is a graph-based web application that visualizes co-citation networks of bioinformatics tools derived from scientific publications available through the imported tools in the OpenEBench (OEB) collection. However, while it captures how tools are cited together, it does not reflect how they are combined in real-world workflows. This information is available in WorkflowHub, a registry of computational workflows with explicit tool compositions mapped to bio.tools identifiers. This project proposes to bridge these two complementary sources through two interconnected tracks. First, we will fetch workflows metadata from WorkflowHub's API, map its composed tools to their bio.tools IDs, identify those not yet registered in OEB and incorporate them into the platform, and introduce workflows themselves as a new entity type in OEB, enabling explicit connections between tools, workflows, and benchmarking activities. Second, we will extend InSoLiTo's graph interface to represent workflows as directed graphs, making it possible to visualize not only which tools are co-cited, but how they connect and in what order, a dimension currently absent from InSoLiTo, allowing users to explore execution paths and better understand tools interoperability in practice. Together, these tracks will lay the groundwork for a unified, multi-source view of bioinformatics tool usage, bridging scientific literature, real-world practice, and research infrastructures.
leads: Juan Crisantos Pérez, Magnus Palmblad, Vedran Kasalica

title: Condeessi a Conda-EESSI transpiler for increased software stack portability, performance and resilience
abstract: Scientific software in the life sciences has been distributed through two major and complementary ecosystems: Bioconda (and Biocontainers) and EESSI, the European Environment for Scientific Software Installations. EESSI provides a shared software stack optimised for high-performance computing, designed for performance and portability across a wide range of processor architectures, from x86 and ARM to RISC-V, built on EasyBuild, a framework for building and installing scientific software on HPC systems. The urgency of bridging these ecosystems has grown sharply following Anaconda's 2024 licensing changes, which introduced commercial licensing requirements for any organisation with 200 or more employees, effectively restricting the use of Anaconda's use at many HPC centres. Major research institutions in Europe have begun phasing out (Ana)conda, accelerating the need for open alternatives. EESSI, built entirely on open-source foundations, is well-positioned to fill this gap. Simultaneously, Bioconda risks being affected by disruptions triggered by these changes. This project aims to develop Condeessi (pronounced "Condessi"), a transpiler tool that facilitates conversion of packaging recipes between the Conda and EasyBuild formats. The primary direction is Conda-to-EESSI, with bidirectional conversion as a longer-term goal. A prototype already exists and validates the feasibility of the approach, though it also reveals its technical complexity. Bioconda has amassed enormous value through thousands of carefully curated, community-maintained recipes. Rather than duplicating this effort in EESSI, Condeessi aims to multiply that investment across ecosystems. Errors or inconsistencies discovered during transpilation will be fed back to Bioconda and Biocontainers as upstream improvements, directly benefiting all three communities.
leads: Renato Alves, Alan O'Cais, Mateo Boudet

title: Towards a semantic artefact catalogue for exposome ontology cross-mapping
abstract: The exposome represents the totality of environmental and endogenous exposures across an individual’s lifetime, encompassing both external and internal components. It has additional spatial and temporal features related to the location, duration, and timing of exposure. This complexity presents significant challenges for integrating exposome data with multi-omics datasets, given the diversity of data types, measurement modalities. Although several initiatives proposed a unified metadata standard and data model for exposome research, interoperability remains limited due to fragmentation across ontologies, disciplines, and regional practices. To address this, we propose a cross-ontology semantic integration approach rather than enforcing a single unified standard. In this project, we develop a semantic artefact catalogue (SAC) that aggregates artefacts across relevant domains, including environmental exposures, toxicology, clinical phenotypes, and lifestyle factors. We then implement a cross-mapping framework to align semantically related concepts across ontologies e.g. ECTO, ChEBI, ENVO, ExO, FoodOn … etc, enabling researchers to use domain-appropriate vocabularies while maintaining interoperability across datasets. We will use OntoPortal as the infrastructure for SAC with artefacts modelled as standardised entities derived from ontologies accessed via OntoPortal APIs. Cross-mapping will be limited to 10-12 ontologies and a prototype use case will be developed. The project is aimed at expanding the activities of Toxicology Community work by applying the FAIRification efforts of the toxicology community to exposome. This will also include building collaborations with different exposome initiatives where INTOXICOM outputs/implementation approaches can be used. SAC will also help intercommunity collaboration due to its various artefact alignments, e.g. metabolomics and pathogen FG
leads: Sara Morsy, Egon Willighagen, Bashir MAYAHI

title: Automated Software Maturity Assessment and Tool Disambiguation in bio.tools
abstract: This project aims to enrich ELIXIR’s bio.tools software registry by applying a new, automated, research software maturity model to the approximately 10,000 tools in bio.tools that are linked to a GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg repository, and are described in at least one publication. The project will evaluate whether automated maturity (e.g., documentation quality, FAIR compliance, maintenance, and reuse signals) assessment can provide a scalable and informative complement to manual maturity annotation and assign up-to-date maturity levels. As a long-term goal, the maturity model will become part of software disambiguation that goes beyond names, descriptions and topics, allowing for more fine-grained searchability among tools with similar functionality, building on the wealth of metadata in the Research Software Ecosystem to assist researchers searching for and making informed selections of software tools. The project combines software metadata from bio.tools and other services of the Research Software Ecosystem, including OpenEBench, repository metadata from code hosting platforms, publication metadata from Europe PMC, and static code analysis using open-source software adapting and building on an automated maturity model recently developed in the more narrowly scoped TDCC-LSH “FAIR Toolbox” project in the Netherlands. The expected outputs are a benchmarked workflow to automatically retrieve relevant metrics from the available information, a first maturity assessment for a large subset of bio.tools, and recommendations for how maturity can be integrated into bio.tools curation and display workflows.
leads: Ana Mendes, Lev Levitsky, Veit Schwämmle

title: Supporting ELIXIR Nodes in maturing RDM services through the Data Stewardship Handbook
abstract: ELIXIR Nodes need practical guidance to consistently organise RDM services in a harmonised way. The [Data Stewardship Handbook & Maturity Model (DSH)](https://elixir-europe.github.io/ds-handbook), currently a beta version, provides the starting point. However, many pages do not yet show how the guidance is applied or how issues are solved in practice. For example, pages on RDM training, expert networks or metadata describe approaches without showing how these are organised at the Node level. This project improves the uptake of DSH within the ELIXIR RDM ecosystem by strengthening the links to existing RDM resources and Platform activities (e.g., RDMkit, FAIR Cookbook, DSW). Participants work on selected Handbook pages and apply them to real situations from their Nodes. They revise content, clarify guidance and integrate examples that reflect existing practices. The page on RDM training, for example, will be developed into a structured page that includes a Node case and links to e.g. TeSS for resources and RDMkit for roles. The metadata page will include links to FAIRsharing for standards, the FAIR Cookbook for implementation recipes and DSW for DM planning support. This collaborative and practice-based approach enables participants with different levels of experience to work together on Handbook pages. The work remains within a clearly defined scope (see below) and delivers publishable updates. It results in reusable Handbook pages that enable Nodes - alongside international communities from multiple disciplines beyond ELIXIR - to move from general guidance to implementation, and to improve their RDM services based on practices tested across ELIXIR.
leads: Mijke Jetten, Hana Marcetic, Jeanne Wilbrandt

title: Open Pathway Maps: Scalable and FAIR Visualization of Metabolic Networks
abstract: Many high-quality metabolic pathway resources provide rich, curated biochemical knowledge, but manually creating biologically meaningful pathway maps remains cumbersome. At the same time, several widely used pathway resources have moved to restrictive licensing models (e.g. KEGG, MetaCyc), limiting open access and reuse. As AI-driven analyses increasingly depend on high-quality reference knowledge, FAIR and openly accessible pathway representations are becoming more important for expert validation, interpretation, and programmatic reuse. This project will advance the systematic evaluation, benchmarking, and future automation of metabolic pathway maps by combining data-driven approaches with expert curation. We will benchmark existing layout strategies, including graph layout methods, constraint-based approaches such as UNICON, and standards-aware tools based on SBML and SBGN, while defining biological and visual requirements for pathway maps. The project brings together contributors from multiple ELIXIR-related resources and provides diverse datasets as input and evaluation benchmarks. Representative pathway maps from BRENDA, Reactome, Metabolic Atlas, and other open resources will serve as reference cases to assess layout quality and identify shared visual principles. Resulting pathway representations will be made available in structured, machine-readable formats to support downstream analyses such as omics data integration. All outcomes are designed for integration into sustainable research infrastructures, including the DSMZ Digital Diversity Hub, Metabolic Atlas, and ELIXIR Node services such as systems biology knowledge graphs supporting SBML and SBGN exports (e.g. the Stress Knowledge Map). This project aims to establish a scalable and FAIR framework for metabolic pathways relevant to systems biology, metabolomics, and plant science.
leads: Julia Koblitz, Sébastien Moretti, Eduard Kerkhoven

title: Single-cell dataset integration across repositories and species for cell type homology analyses
abstract: Single-cell data are rapidly increasing both in quantity and diversity; however, clear reporting standards have not yet been adopted across the field. This leads to multiple non-compatible practices across datasets and resources, limits reusability, and makes it difficult to retrieve, integrate, and interpret data in a robust way. In parallel, comparative single-cell atlases are creating unprecedented opportunities to study cell type evolution across species. Yet robust cell type homology inference remains challenging because results depend strongly on upstream choices, including preprocessing, annotation granularity, and the homology relationships used to connect genes across species. Several groups are already collaborating on these issues under the umbrella of the scFAIR consortium, including CELLxGENE, EMBL-EBI Single Cell Expression Atlas, Bgee, ASAP, Alliance of Genome Resources. We propose to leverage their foundational work regarding common metadata schema and aggregation of datasets across resources, and to extend it for improving multi-species analyses, and cell population matching. Our overall aim is to improve dataset integration across resources and species, to shed light on cell population determination mechanisms. During this BioHackathon, we propose to develop 3 work packages, benefiting from the diversity of skillsets among participants. I) biodata resource component: to develop adaptors to query and integrate datasets annotated in multiple ELIXIR biodata resources and beyond. II) Tool benchmarking component: to benchmark how pre-processing choices impact analysis results and mappability, notably across species. III) Cell biology component: to investigate homologous and lineage-specific cell types to identify cell innovations or incomplete atlas coverage.
leads: Frederic Bastian, Sabrina Jagot, Samantha Smith

title: Evaluating and Securing AI-Assisted Workflows for Sensitive Data
abstract: Handling sensitive data in cloud environments presents a significant challenge: researchers need flexible analysis tools while data custodians must ensure privacy and prevent data exfiltration. Lately, coding agents became popular and are being used for many tasks, including workflow creation. The idea of automatic code generation for sensitive data processing evokes immediate security concerns. Workflow execution in a secure environment must fulfill certain safety standards and requires deterministic behavior. This project aims to deliver best practices and safety guidelines regarding code generating AI tools in Secure Processing Environments. As part of the process, a pilot platform will be created to find vulnerabilities, develop countermeasures and validate them. In this proposed platform, an agent system is used for code generation and for monitoring data integrity. Users interact with an agent that has access to necessary tools and metadata, and constructs a Snakemake workflow based on the user's needs. To ensure reproducibility and security, the workflow is executed deterministically via WESkit, running independently of the agent. Results will be documented using RO-crates. A separate security validation agent, augmented with deterministic static code analysis tools, reviews the code to prevent harmful code execution. It applies standard Data Loss Prevention filters before sharing them with the user. Ideally, the steps required to ensure secure workflow execution are formalized in such a way that they can be followed autonomously. The goal of this BioHackathon project is to prototype this platform, actively conduct security testing to identify potential vulnerabilities and develop best practices for AI-driven SPEs.
leads: Landfried Kraatz, Fotis Psomopoulos, Theodoros Katzalis

title: DBTLHUB Interoperability Contracts: Standardised Phase Transitions for Engineering Biology
abstract: DBTL workflows in engineering biology remain fragmented at phase transition points. Tools for design, build, test, and learn excel within their domains, but the exchange of outputs, metadata, provenance, and quality information between phases is inconsistent, often manual, and poorly standardised. This creates unnecessary friction for researchers trying to connect existing resources into coherent workflows. This project defines a lightweight interoperability contract for DBTL phase transitions, delivering concrete schemas for Design→Build (construct specifications), Build→Test (assembly outputs), Test→Learn (phenotypic screening data), and Learn→Design (model predictions). Each schema specifies minimum artefacts, metadata requirements, provenance tracking, and quality signals needed for reliable handovers. We will implement a minimal OpenAPI service and reference output wrappers/adapters specifications, demonstrating how tool outputs convert to standardised handover packages. A demonstrator workflow will validate end-to-end exchange across at least two transitions. The approach makes phase handovers machine-readable and reusable without requiring tools to be rewritten. Outputs integrate naturally with ELIXIR services (bio.tools, Galaxy) and provide a practical foundation for DBTLHUB's one-stop resource hub. The result is a reusable specification that reduces manual reformatting, improves reproducibility, and clarifies how heterogeneous DBTL tools connect into working workflows, establishing a concrete interoperability layer for engineering biology that scales with community adoption.
leads: Oscar Dias, Vitor Martins dos Santos, Anil Wipat

title: Who does what in ELIXIR? Building an agent-driven, low-maintenance "ELIXIR Atlas."
abstract: ELIXIR coordinates hundreds of people across platforms, communities, nodes, and focus groups. The information describing this ecosystem – who does what, how activities relate – is scattered across programme documents, websites, registries, and institutional knowledge. For newcomers and participants alike, understanding the full landscape is difficult. For coordinators, detecting overlaps or gaps across platforms requires manually cross-referencing large document sets. The reason this problem persists is lack of ownership: no single party is responsible for an integrated landscape view, and there is no dedicated funding for one. Manual integration efforts cannot be sustained at this scale. We propose building a public, queryable knowledge graph of the ELIXIR ecosystem in which both creation and maintenance are agent-driven – the ELIXIR Atlas. Using BioCypher and an agentic ingestion pipeline (LLM-driven extraction with human-in-the-loop validation), the Atlas integrates publicly available information – programme texts, bio.tools, FAIRsharing, TeSS, the ELIXIR website – into a structured representation of platforms, activities, people, services, and their relationships. The agent-driven design is the central contribution: it dramatically lowers the human effort required to keep the Atlas current as the programme evolves, making the resource sustainable without a dedicated curation team. The hackathon will deliver a minimum viable product from public sources only. This MVP is intended to demonstrate value to ELIXIR stakeholders and unlock access to internal documents in subsequent phases. The methodology has been validated in adjacent settings, and early prototypes indicate it can scale to ecosystems of this complexity – making this the right moment to apply it to ELIXIR.
leads: Sebastian Lobentanzer, Xènia Pérez Sitjà, Shoaib Ahmed Sufi

title: Expanding the ELIXIR TES Network with Life-Science Services
abstract: The ELIXIR On-Cloud TES network provides a functional GA4GH TES environment for federated task execution across ELIXIR Nodes. Building on this foundation, we propose a BioHackathon project that aims to leverage the TES network to deploy research services, similar to what has been done for the BioHackCloud (https://biohack.cloud/services), but via TES requests. Such TES-deployed services could support progress in other ELIXIR initiatives, including compute provenance efforts such as ELIXIR-STEERS, secrets management (e.g. OpenBao), and other service integrations such as Galaxy workflow execution in the TES network. More broadly, the project aims to show how the TES network can serve as an execution layer for research services. The resulting services will be linked and documented at the BioHackCloud and thus made available to the BioHack community. This project directly operationalises the ELIXIR On-Cloud roadmap by using TES as a common interoperability layer not only for task submission but also for interactive life-science analysis services. It contributes a concrete, user-facing use case to the established TES ecosystem, documentation, and best-practice portfolio. The minimal viable deliverable will demonstrate a complete execution path: user request > TES task dispatch via proTES > service/task execution on a federated node > interactive result delivery.
leads: Valentin Schneider-Lunitz, Alexander Kanitz, Pavel Nikonorov

title: WeatherXBiodiversity: Exploring Harmonization of Cross-Domain Data into FAIR Digital Objects
abstract: Climate change is one of the major challenges of the coming years, with particularly serious impacts on biodiversity. Understanding and responding to these impacts increasingly depends on combining data from different scientific domains, especially biodiversity observations and climate data. Both kinds of data are abundant and openly available, but they are not readily aligned: they use different metadata models, conventions, and publication pathways, making them difficult to combine in a reproducible and reusable way. At the same time, technologies such as RO-Crate now exist to package such multimodal data, workflows, and provenance into FAIR digital objects (FDOs). However, when assembling cross-domain research objects from heterogeneous sources, researchers need additional support with structuring, annotating, and harmonizing the metadata. This project will address that need by developing a reusable approach for combining cross-domain data into a unified FDO. The Annotated Research Context (ARC) framework will provide the working environment for organising data, workflows, and workflow executions, which can be represented as an RO-Crate for exchange and publication. As a concrete use case, we will combine bumblebee occurrence records from GBIF with ERA5 gridded climate data to reproduce the European component of Soroye, Newbold and Kerr (2020) on climate-driven bumblebee decline. The main outcome is not a new ecological result, but a reusable FDO, including empiric data, structured experimental and administrative metadata and executable workflows described through CWL. With the knowledge gained, we aim to deliver reusable templates, and accompanying training materials that others can adapt to related biodiversity–climate studies.
leads: Anne Fouilloux, Paul Slavin, Heinrich Lukas Weil

title: A gender-informed bibliometric index to amplify underrepresented voices in ELIXIR publications
abstract: Gender representation in scholarly publications remains a critical challenge in Life Sciences, where women authors, particularly as leading contributors, are systematically underrepresented. Bibliographic information retrieval systems such as Google Scholar, despite their widespread use, operate through opaque ranking algorithms that may further amplify such biases, reducing the visibility of female-led research. Building on work initiated at BioHackathon Europe 2024 and refined over the past two years, this project leverages a gender-aware bibliographic retrieval workflow developed by the Bioinfo4Women initiative at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). The system automatically retrieves publication metadata and infers author gender, enabling systematic analysis of gender bias in scholarly visibility. The current project extends this foundation by introducing a novel bibliographic ranking index that incorporates gender as an explicit parameter alongside conventional metrics such as citation counts, h-index, and impact factor. The goal is to surface the contributions of underrepresented female authors across Life Sciences domains, allowing their work to emerge beyond what traditional ranking systems would otherwise permit. The use case is the curated set of >3,000 ELIXIR-supported publications compiled by the ELIXIR Impact Group. Bibliographic parameters will be retrieved efficiently through the BIP! Services (https://bip.imis.athena-innovation.gr/), developed by the ELIXIR Greece node. This effort directly aligns with ongoing ELIXIR Hub initiatives to systematically identify ELIXIR contributions across publications, projects, and training activities, and connects to BSC's sustained co-leadership of the ELIXIR ELEAD initiative focused on women's leadership in Life Sciences.
leads: Davide Cirillo, Claudia Rosas, Eva Alloza

title: BiCoReCa (Biodiversity Community Resource Catalogue): Towards Centralized Curation and Integration
abstract: The rapid growth of biodiversity research has led to the development of numerous bioinformatics tools and databases, information about which remains fragmented across disparate cataloging efforts, hindering resource discovery and utilization. To address this gap, we offer the development of BiCoReCa (Biodiversity Community Resource Catalogue), a comprehensive, dynamic, open-access catalogue of biodiversity-related bioinformatics resources (tools, workflows, training, standards, and databases). Our team leverages successful prior ELIXIR BioHackathon experience, building upon lessons from developing Galaxy CoDex and a related initiative MiCoReCa. This demonstrates our capability to execute the BiCoReCa initiative and deliver impactful outcomes. The BiCoReCa catalogue's framework will be designed for transferability, enabling integration into platforms like Galaxy and other open-source initiatives. This initiative will utilize EDAM and cross-reference established registries like bio.tools and WorkflowHub to create a centralized, FAIR inventory. A key feature is the community-driven process for identifying and curating missing ontological terms and metadata, ensuring BiCoReCa's accuracy and relevance in collaboration with partner efforts. Furthermore, the catalogue will integrate links to training materials from TeSS to support appropriate tool usage, and connect with OpenEBench for benchmarking capabilities. This project will provide a vital resource for the biodiversity field, enhancing research efficiency and reproducibility. It will also establish a sustainable, adaptable infrastructure potentially applicable to other communities, such as Single-Cell Omics in ELIXIR or image data workflows in Euro-BioImaging, who also showed interest in this initiative. This effort represents a significant contribution by the ELIXIR Biodiversity Community and the Tools Platform to streamline findability within biodiversity informatics.
leads: Clara Emery, Solenne Correard, Matúš Kalaš

title: Nextflow to Galaxy Workflow Portability and FAIRness via Modular LLM Agent Skills
abstract: Computational workflows encode domain expertise and operating procedures, and large, curated catalogues of production pipelines have emerged, such as nf-core for Nextflow and the Intergalactic Workflow Commission (IWC) for Galaxy. However, the reimplementation of these assets across languages remains a mostly-manual, resource-heavy work, and thus a bottleneck for FAIR, reproducible science. To improve workflow portability between Nextflow and Galaxy, we propose a "maturation ladder", based on Large Language Model (LLM) agent skills: * Translation: A Nextflow to Galaxy porting skill (via CWL), extending recently developed work . * Prototyping: On-the-fly user-defined tools (UDTs) that wrap missing tools or custom nf-core scripts, making ports immediately end-to-end runnable. * Hardening: A tool-authoring skill that promotes UDTs into standard, best-practice Galaxy tools ready for community review, providing reusable wrappers rather than throwaway glue. * Maintenance: A sync mechanism that keeps ported pipelines and wrapped tools in lockstep with upstream nf-core releases. To ensure high standards, we will extend the existing Galaxy workflow Best Practice panel with an LLM-based FAIRness evaluator. While the current panel checks for basic metadata, our extension will leverage LLMs to evaluate deeper criteria from established community principles (e.g. 10.1038/s41597-025-04451-9 ), providing actionable feedback for both new ports and existing workflows. These capabilities will be exposed via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for any agent or CLI, and as a ChatGXY plugin inside Galaxy's web interface. This modular architecture decomposes the complex translation task into smaller, parallelisable components, allowing diverse teams to contribute simultaneously towards a more unified and FAIR bioinformatics ecosystem.
leads: Nicola Soranzo, Martin Cech, Marius van den Beek
